original_question: Do there exist polytopes P and Q such that the amalgamation class hP, Qi is nonempty and P has at least two non-isomorphic vertex-figures?
target_in_paper: The draft is aiming at the paper’s open problem in its final combinatorial-constructions discussion that asks whether the amalgamation notation ⟨P,Q⟩ can be meaningfully realized when the prescribed facet type P is not vertex-figure-homogeneous, i.e. when P itself has more than one isomorphism type of vertex-figure.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core existence question, uses the paper’s amalgamation-class notation ⟨P,Q⟩, and correctly focuses on the exceptional case where the prescribed facet polytope P has at least two non-isomorphic vertex-figures.
missing_details: The paper is about abstract polytopes, not convex or geometric polytopes.
The ranks should be made explicit: P and Q are abstract n-polytopes, and ⟨P,Q⟩ denotes a class of abstract (n+1)-polytopes.
The notation ⟨P,Q⟩ should be defined in the question itself: it is the class of abstract (n+1)-polytopes whose facets are all isomorphic to P and whose vertex-figures are all isomorphic to Q.
It should be stated that 'P has at least two non-isomorphic vertex-figures' means that vertex-figures at different vertices of P are not all mutually isomorphic as abstract polytopes.
An implicit lower-rank restriction is needed: n ≥ 3, since otherwise P cannot have multiple vertex-figure types in the intended sense.
The question is purely existential; no finiteness, regularity, chirality, or realizability hypotheses should be added.
refined_question: Do there exist abstract n-polytopes P and Q, with n ≥ 3, such that the amalgamation class ⟨P,Q⟩ is nonempty—that is, there exists an abstract (n+1)-polytope all of whose facets are isomorphic to P and all of whose vertex-figures are isomorphic to Q—even though P itself has at least two pairwise non-isomorphic vertex-figures?
justification: The draft is already very close to the paper’s intended open problem: it preserves the paper’s amalgamation-class notation and isolates exactly the phenomenon the authors are asking about, namely whether amalgamation can occur when the prescribed facet type P is not uniform in its own vertex-figures. What needed sharpening was only the ambient setting and notation: the paper works with abstract polytopes, ⟨P,Q⟩ is a class of rank-one-higher amalgamations, and the phrase about non-isomorphic vertex-figures refers to the internal local structure of P itself. This paper is a survey of open problems rather than a theorem-driven article, so the right target is the relevant open problem in the final combinatorial-constructions section, not a broader neighboring question about universal extensions or flat amalgamation in general.
